worksheet.title: Loops That Make Patterns
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.1 — repeating events
worksheet.learning_goal: I can use a repeat loop to make a pattern that repeats.

parts.title: Patterns repeat
text: Look at a striped shirt or a bead bracelet — the same part shows up again and again. That is a pattern.
A repeat loop runs ALL the blocks inside it each time around. So if you put two stamps inside, the loop makes a repeating pattern for you. Watch Bit make a bead pattern.

parts.title: Read this loop
parts.note: Both stamps run each time. 3 repeats of (red, blue) makes 6 beads: red, blue, red, blue, red, blue.

parts.caption: Bit stamps red, blue — and the loop repeats it 3 times.

parts.title: Count it
parts.prompt: The loop repeats 3 times and stamps 2 beads each time. How many beads each repeat? ______  How many beads in TOTAL? ______

parts.title: Predict, then check
parts.prompt: Change repeat 3 to repeat 4. PREDICT how many beads Bit makes now, then CHECK by counting 2 for each repeat. How many beads?

parts.title: Write your own
parts.prompt: Make Bit stamp a heart-then-star pattern 5 times. Write the repeat number:  repeat ______ → ( stamp heart, stamp star )

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Now there are THREE stamps inside:  repeat 3 → ( ●, ▲, ■ ). How many stamps in total? Draw what the pattern looks like.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A loop repeats the WHOLE inside each time. The blocks inside are one piece of the pattern — repeat them to make the pattern grow.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: A repeat loop runs EVERY block inside it each time, so a loop with two or more actions builds a repeating pattern. Students count, change, and write pattern loops. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the blocks and what Bit does, so you can teach from the printout. Optional: a Scratch-style app to drag the blocks and watch Bit run — you only press the green flag.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). The loop stamps 2 beads each time; 3 repeats make 6 beads.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — 2 beads each repeat, 6 in total.
3. Let them work. Students predict the change (Ex 2), write a repeat (Ex 3), and count a three-stamp loop (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — 2 beads each repeat; 6 beads total (2 × 3). Exercise 2 — 8 beads (2 × 4); predict 8.
Exercise 3 — repeat 5 (makes 10 stamps). Exercise 4 (challenge) — 9 stamps (3 × 3); the pattern is heart-star-square, three times.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: counting only one block per repeat. Every block inside runs each time.
Make it easier: circle the blocks inside the loop, then multiply by the repeat number.
Make it harder: ask the total for a four-stamp loop repeated 3 times (12).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change one, and explain what the change did to the result.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child multiplies the blocks inside by the repeat number to find the total.
